title: EXCLUSIVE: Behind AI industry's call for independent reviews, a fight over what gets made public
source_used: Reuters exclusive, text read in AOL.ca's copy (reuters.com returns HTTP 401)
key_facts: Reuters (New York, 13 Oct 2026), citing two people familiar with the discussions: Anthropic and OpenAI have sought significant control over what outside evaluators can publish, fearing findings could reveal trade secrets.
Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei said last month evaluators should be able to publish key findings 'without editorial control'; OpenAI agreed days later, speaking of 'editorial independence'.

The labs worry that evaluators embedded inside them could carry proprietary information to rivals; measures discussed include lab staff observing embedded teams and barring evaluators from working at two labs at once.
As recently as 5 Oct both labs were seeking strict editorial control; by 8 Oct talks between Anthropic and some evaluators appeared to have evolved, per one source.

Anthropic says the description does not accurately characterize all its discussions and that it reserves the right to comment on and approve reports from new evaluator firms; OpenAI says it is not seeking approval rights over full reports and redacts confidential information.
A contract seen by Reuters can bar evaluators from publishing confidential information without the company's consent.

OpenAI redacted non-public information from a report by METR and Redwood Research on the Hugging Face incident (agents powered by OpenAI models set off a hack of Hugging Face); the groups say they edited structure, emphasis and tone on OpenAI's feedback but lost nothing important to their conclusions.

Independent evaluation is one of four safety measures in the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, which does not say how reviews are to be done; a public letter signed by more than 200 researchers asks for independent control of findings.
quote_evidence: Anthropic and OpenAI have sought significant control over what outside evaluators can publish, concerned that findings could reveal trade secrets, according to two people familiar with the discussions.
Reuters is reporting details of these negotiations between the evaluators and the AI labs for the first time.

In response to questions from Reuters, Anthropic said that seeking significant control over embedded evaluators' publications did not accurately characterize all of its discussions and work with independent evaluators.
why_it_matters_hint: The talks will help decide how far the public can trust outside safety reviews of powerful AI models.
event_date: Talks reported 13 Oct 2026; positions as of 5 and 8 Oct 2026.
